ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A, contrasted with long, structured presentation turns. Overlap and interruptions are light but frequent in the form of quick acknowledgments, repeated “yeah,” greetings, and speakers starting before a previous thought fully lands. Participants hedge often with “um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” and self-corrections; many questions are framed tentatively as “I have a naive question,” “do you think,” or “have you looked at.” Formality is moderate: introductions and transitions are polished, while the surrounding conversation is warm, informal, and filled with friendly praise. Speakers build on prior remarks by restating part of a point before extending it, and challenges are indirect, usually posed as open questions or alternative possibilities rather than disagreement. Notable patterns include false starts, repetitions, fragmented syntax, technical shorthand, and supportive backchanneling; Q&A often begins with praise, then a multipart question, followed by exploratory rather than definitive answers.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Planning how to raise school-entry vaccination rates in a county that has recently experienced a measles cluster.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a postdoctoral infectious-disease epidemiologist with 4 years of applied work in state and county health departments following doctoral training in spatial epidemiology. She has analyzed measles and pertussis investigations using line lists, school reporting files, immunization-registry extracts, and geocoded service-access measures. Her work includes estimating coverage under incomplete reporting, assessing registry-record linkage quality, mapping clusters without publishing identifiable small-area results, and separating vaccination documentation status from plausible population protection.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya frames the problem first as one of measurement and transmission risk: the 18 linked cases, the two adjacent school catchments, and the schools below 88% documentation may indicate meaningful clustering, but reporting lags, duplicate or unmatched registry records, and exemptions or records obtained elsewhere can distort apparent coverage. She will press the group to define denominators, quantify missingness, compare school submissions with registry and clinic records, and avoid treating documented MMR status as a direct measure of immunity. She is skeptical that messaging or engagement strategies can be judged by anecdote alone, and asks for a feasible evaluation design with timely, disaggregated-but-protected outcomes such as verified on-time MMR documentation, completed referrals, and post-registration gaps.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Luis Ramirez, MPH
speakers.background: Luis is Pine County Health Department's immunization program manager and has 11 years of experience running childhood-vaccination operations, including outbreak response, vaccine ordering, clinic staffing, and school-health coordination. He manages two evening immunization-clinic slots per week, a small outreach budget, and data-sharing workflows involving the state registry, county clinics, and school nursing staff. During the measles response he coordinated case-related vaccination referrals and saw how quickly nurse follow-up time became the limiting resource.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis treats the planning question as an implementation and service-delivery problem under a four-month deadline. He focuses on who can receive, reconcile, and act on school documentation; whether referral pathways produce appointments and completed doses; what can realistically fit within the two evening clinic sessions; and which activities would shift burden onto already stretched school nurses. He wants an actionable workflow that uses existing administrative records without creating an unmanageable call-and-chase system. He can identify operational indicators—referrals issued, appointments offered, appointment completion, record resolution time, and staff hours—but is uncertain how much evidence from other locations predicts uptake in Pine County's particular communities.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is a medical sociologist and research project manager with 9 years of experience studying family health decisions, institutional trust, and community-based public-health partnerships. Her mixed-methods work has included interviews with parents and frontline staff, focus groups designed with community organizations, observation of school and clinic interactions, and surveys of information networks and service barriers. She has managed projects involving sensitive administrative data and has experience developing consent, confidentiality, and non-stigmatizing recruitment procedures with local partners.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Aisha emphasizes that a missing vaccination record and a delayed vaccination can arise through very different social processes: work schedules and transportation, fragmented care, confusing administrative requirements, prior experiences of disrespect, distrust of public agencies, safety concerns, or influence from peer and faith networks. She cautions that identifying two catchments or low-documentation schools as high priority can unintentionally label families or neighborhoods as irresponsible, weakening the trust needed for participation. She asks the group to distinguish access barriers from confidence and relationship barriers, to involve parent and community intermediaries in interpreting findings, and to assess whether communications or referral processes are experienced as supportive rather than punitive. She favors collecting only information necessary for planning and evaluation, using aggregate reporting and carefully governed linkages where individual-level records are needed.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

meeting_opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Convene a planning meeting among an epidemiologist, a county public-health program manager, and a sociologist. The epidemiologist should describe the geographic and school-level clustering of under-vaccination, the recent outbreak data, uncertainty caused by reporting lag and incomplete registry matching, and the need to distinguish documented coverage from actual immunity. The public-health manager should describe operational constraints: two evening clinic slots per week, finite outreach funds, school-nurse workload, available administrative records, and the need for an actionable plan before registration. The sociologist should describe the importance of family decision-making, institutional trust, peer and community networks, and the risk that a targeted campaign could stigmatize families. Participants should discuss what evidence would be needed to select and evaluate interventions, including feasible data sources and privacy constraints. They may define needed outcomes and constraints, but they must not select a final intervention package or claim that any proposed method is validated for this county. The meeting should leave open which methods to use and how to combine them.

reference_methods.method: Small-area descriptive analysis and geospatial mapping of school-entry MMR documentation, outbreak cases, registry completeness, and access indicators.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Can identify susceptible pockets and prioritize schools or neighborhoods while making uncertainty from incomplete records and surveillance lag visible.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Maps should use aggregated or privacy-protected data and must not treat missing documentation as definite non-vaccination.

reference_methods.method: Retrospective cohort or record-linkage analysis using school submissions, immunization registry records, and clinic records.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Can estimate timely vaccination and documentation completion, characterize gaps, and assess whether outreach or clinic access is associated with school-entry completion.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Requires careful deduplication, definitions of valid doses and exemptions, and attention to selection bias and delayed reporting.

reference_methods.method: Rapid implementation assessment using workflow mapping and structured interviews with school nurses, clinic staff, pediatric practices, and community partners.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Can locate bottlenecks in record review, referral, appointment scheduling, transport, clinic hours, and follow-up before committing scarce staff time.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Operational reports should be triangulated with administrative data and include representatives from the high-need school areas.

reference_methods.method: Pragmatic pilot or phased implementation evaluation of feasible service changes, such as extended clinics, reminder-referral workflows, or school-linked vaccination access.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Allows the county to compare reach, completion, equity, cost, and burden under real staffing and budget constraints before scaling.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Phasing should be ethically justified and evaluation should account for differences between schools rather than assuming simple before-and-after changes prove impact.

reference_methods.method: Semi-structured interviews and focus groups with parents or caregivers, school nurses, clinicians, and trusted community messengers.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Can examine how families make vaccination decisions, experience access barriers, interpret risk, and decide which institutions and messengers are credible.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Recruitment should include vaccinated, delayed, and undocumented families where possible, use non-stigmatizing language, and protect participants from perceived school or health-department pressure.

reference_methods.method: Community-network or stakeholder mapping, supplemented by qualitative analysis of information pathways.
reference_methods.fit_to_problem: Can identify trusted connectors and channels through which concerns and accurate information circulate, helping tailor outreach without assuming one message works for all families.
reference_methods.key_caveat: Network information should not be used to label communities as resistant; consent, confidentiality, and community review are important.

ground_truth.cross_disciplinary_design: A mixed-methods design could first use epidemiologic mapping and linked administrative records to identify patterns and data-quality gaps; use workflow assessment to establish feasible delivery options; then use qualitative and network-informed inquiry to interpret barriers, trust, and messenger choices. A pragmatic pilot can evaluate selected options using agreed outcomes such as valid MMR completion by registration, time from referral to vaccination, reach across schools, missed-opportunity rates, staff burden, cost, and family-reported acceptability.
ground_truth.expert_review_needed: Epidemiology, immunization-program, school-health, privacy/legal, community-engagement, and qualitative-methods experts should review data linkage, case and coverage definitions, equity safeguards, recruitment, interpretation, and causal claims before methods or interventions are finalized.

seed_location: The seed conditions are substantially present across turns 1-30, though not every requested operational detail is explicit. Epidemiologic context appears in turns 2, 4, 6, 13, 19, 22, and 29: delayed registry uploads, incomplete matching/duplicates, valid-dose rules, distinction between documentation and vaccination, school-level differences (93% county documentation vs. below 88% in three schools), and 18 linked outbreak cases concentrated in the relevant catchments. Public-health operational constraints appear in turns 1, 3-5, 9, 11, 15, 17, 20, 23, 26, 28, and 30: nurse workload, appointment/no-show capacity, clinic flow, finite staffing, records access, a fixed outreach cap, and the registration timeline. The explicit seed detail of two evening clinic slots per week and finite outreach funds is not stated; turn 17/28 refers only to 'two evening clinics' and staffing. Sociological concerns appear in turns 7, 10, 12, 14-16, 18, 21, 24, and 27: trust in messengers, family barriers and decisions, peer/community connectors, communication channels, non-stigmatization, voluntary/opt-in contact, and avoiding enrollment pressure. Evidence, data sources, and privacy constraints are discussed in turns 3-6, 9-16, 20-24, and 27-29, including named reconciliation, registry/school/appointment data, de-identified wording review, aggregate engagement data, retention limits, permissions, and confidentiality safeguards. The group does not finalize an intervention package or claim validation for the county; it leaves the feasible outreach route and cap conditional on reconciliation, staffing, permissions, and review (turns 26-30).

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: Morning—hope everybody stayed dry this weekend. The rain was a mess on my side of the county. I know we’re tight on time, so I’d like to get clear on whether we can separate missing paperwork from actually missing doses in those three schools before we build a follow-up process that the—before we build something the nurses can’t sustain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The rain was brutal. On the records question, I'd be careful about calling a school-file gap a dose gap. During the outbreak reconciliation, some of those records showed up in the registry only after delayed provider uploads. Luis, do you have a sense of where the school-to-clinic path is actually—where it's stalling most often, review, referral, getting the appointment, or proof getting back to the school?

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: During the response, the first break looked like school review and proof getting back. Families would show up with records we didn’t have. But after we made referrals, no-shows were the other big drop-off. I don’t have clean counts by step, though. Maya, could we link the school gap to registry status and then, um, appointment outcomes, even just as a pilot for the three schools?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: As a tightly governed pilot, I think so. We'd need to define the school-file denominator and valid-dose rules first, then measure match and delayed-upload rates by school and provider. Otherwise, an apparent improvement could just be paperwork, paperwork catching up. Could we get identifiers and permission for a limited reconciliation before we add appointment outcomes?

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: I can get the school leads’ sign-off for a limited, named reconciliation if we keep it to the three schools and have a clear retention window. I’d want the output to sort people into “record found,” “dose likely needed,” and “still unresolved,” rather than handing nurses another raw exception list. Can you estimate how many will remain in that, that last bucket?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can estimate it, but I wouldn't put a number on the unresolved group until we see the match rate and how long providers are taking to upload. We can make the pilot output those three categories, plus, plus a reason code for unresolved. No registry match, possible duplicate, invalid or incomplete dose history. That way we know whether it's really a follow-up burden or a records problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: I’d keep that unresolved category very tightly held. Before any family follow-up, could nurses note, even briefly, where they think the handoff failed? A missing record and a missed appointment may need completely different outreach, and we shouldn’t let the three-school pilot turn into a label for those families.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, yeah, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: I think a brief nurse note can work if it's structured. Like, not a narrative field, just "record seen by family," "referral made," "appointment missed," or "unknown." Aisha, what's the least intrusive way to ask- how do we ask the unresolved families what got in the way without turning nurses into interviewers?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: I'd keep that separate from the school contact, if we can. A very short voluntary call or text from a trusted clinic, parent group, or community partner could ask one or two practical questions. Was it records, getting an appointment, transport or hours, or something else? And make clear it doesn't affect enrollment. But I'd want to check which messengers families actually trust before we assume the school is the right sender.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: Keeping it separate from enrollment makes sense, because otherwise it’ll read as enforcement no matter how we phrase it. My practical question is who can make those contacts without creating a second queue. Could we test a small text-first outreach from the clinic, with an opt-in call, and track whether it actually- whether it converts to an appointment or a record upload?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Maybe, but I’d be cautious about treating conversion as the only outcome. Some families may resolve a registry or provider-record issue without booking our clinic. Could the text offer a neutral records-help or appointment option, and then- could we use only aggregate results for the pilot? We also need a sender families recognize. I don’t know yet whether the clinic name has that trust in all three school communities.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Aggregate pilot results are fine for the engagement piece, but internally we still need the named reconciliation to know what changed. With county documentation at 93% and those three schools below 88%, I'd report them separately. A verified valid record, a new documented dose, and an appointment completed. Otherwise we'll call a record upload a vaccination gain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: And alongside those internal measures, I’d want one light-touch indicator of whether the contact felt usable rather than, um, pressuring people. Luis, do the clinics or pediatric offices have anyone who could sanity-check the text wording with a few parent or faith-group connectors before it goes out? The same notice can land very differently depending on who it comes from.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: I think so, but I’d need to check capacity before promising it. The pediatric offices may be the better first ask. They already have parent-facing staff, and we could have a couple of connectors react to the wording. Not- I wouldn’t hand them a family list, because I don’t want that review itself to expose who’s unresolved.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: That seems like the right boundary. The wording review can be de-identified and framed around clarity and tone, not around persuading anyone. I’d also ask whether text is even a workable channel for parents with changing numbers or limited data plans. We may need a parallel option through the offices, or a general records-help line.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: A general records-help line might actually catch families who already have the dose but are stuck on the upload piece. I need to check whether we can staff it without pulling from the two evening clinics, though. Maybe offices can route their own patients there, and we keep the clinic text to a very small pilot first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Hm, staffing's the constraint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And staffing's why I'd keep the first pilot very narrow. Three schools, a fixed window, and no assumption that every unresolved record gets a call. Given the 18 linked cases were concentrated around those catchments, it makes sense to prioritize them, but I don't want the outreach list- I don't want it to become a proxy risk label.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: We can prioritize the schools for reconciliation without telling families they're on some outbreak list. Operationally, I'd cap outreach at a fixed number each week, and we'd stop if it starts taking nurse time away from actual clinic flow. The pilot needs to show us resolution by route, not just generate more names.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: I’m comfortable with a cap, as long as the stop rule isn’t just clinic flow. If people are replying that the message feels like a school warning, that’s a signal to pause too. Could the opt-in reply categories give us a very small, aggregate read on records help versus appointment access versus something we haven’t anticipated, or…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Those categories are useful, but they need an “other or prefer not to say” option, and we should not infer a reason from no reply. The 18 linked cases give us a reason to focus the pilot in those catchments, not to treat a text response as a measure of vaccine intent.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: And for our side, no reply just stays unresolved, nothing more. If Maya can give us the weekly counts by those three record categories, I can check the actual appointment slots and nurse hours against a small text-first cap. I just, just don't want us opening up a route we can't carry through.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Before we launch even a small cap, I’d want a couple of parent-facing staff or connectors to look at the opt-in wording and the reply categories, using just de-identified examples. And if people choose “other,” we should have a safe way to surface recurring barriers in aggregate without asking them to explain themselves to the school.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Right, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: I’ll check today what staff coverage and no-show capacity look like for a small weekly cap, and whether the offices can field the records-help route for their own families. Then we can make the pilot stop rule concrete. Sorry, I lost my thread there. Nurse hours, clinic disruption, and any concerning feedback from the replies.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: That works. I’d just add that the feedback stop rule needs a named review point, and somebody outside the outreach workflow should read the aggregate “other” responses, so a concerning pattern doesn’t get dismissed as just low uptake. I can look at the draft consent and message language once Luis knows which route is actually feasible, and then...

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: Once I know whether we can spare, say, a small fixed batch each week without displacing evening appointments, I’ll send over the feasible route and cap. Then Aisha can look at the language before anything goes live. I also need Maya’s rough timing for the first reconciliation output, because that tells us whether we have enough runway before registration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can turn the first reconciliation around in about two weeks once the identifiers and registry permissions are in place. Though I need to check match completeness by provider before I treat it as final. That still leaves runway before registration, and the 18 linked cases, I’ll keep those as context for prioritizing the catchments, not in anything family-facing.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ramirez, MPH
transcript.text: Two weeks works, assuming the permissions don't slip. I'll get the three school leads moving on that today and check the evening-slot and nurse-hour numbers. Then we can- we'll pick this back up once we know what the reconciliation leaves us, because I've got to jump too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think we’ve got enough for today. Thanks, both. Once the permissions piece is moving, I’ll start on the reconciliation. Talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: All right, take care, both.

issues: The transcript does not provide enough evidence for the epidemiology reference method of small-area descriptive analysis/geospatial mapping. Maya mentions three schools, documentation percentages, catchments, and 18 linked cases (turns 13, 19, 22, 29), but nobody proposes mapping school-entry documentation, cases, registry completeness, or access indicators, nor discusses privacy-protected mapping.

The operational evidence-gathering method is underdeveloped. There is no clear workflow mapping or structured interview plan involving school nurses, clinic staff, pediatric practices, and community partners; turns 1-3 and 7-9 identify possible workflow failures, but the meeting jumps quickly to a reconciliation and text-outreach pilot rather than defining a rapid implementation assessment.

The sociological methods are only partially recoverable. Aisha raises trust, messenger choice, stigma, and de-identified wording review (turns 10, 12, 14, 16, 21, 24, 27), but does not clearly propose semi-structured interviews, focus groups, or community/stakeholder-network mapping that would examine family decision-making, peer networks, and information pathways.
